design_detail: Anonymous online cross-sectional survey: the research group's annual survey of drug use among people associated with the dance-music scene, promoted through a collaboration with the dance-music magazine Mixmag on the website dontstayin.com (BJU International 2012; read as the online-first PDF, pages numbered 1–5; the reference record gives the issue pages 110(11):1762–1766). Field period November 2009 to January 2010 by the abstract (the Results print 17 November 2010 to 4 January 2010). Of 3806 completed surveys, the 1285 respondents who reported ketamine use in the last 12 months answered further questions: typical and maximum amounts per session, maximum consecutive days of use, days of use in the last month, a proxy for dependence built from the seven DSM-IV criteria, five urinary symptoms they associated with ketamine in the last 12 months, how the symptoms changed in relation to their use, and help-seeking. Analysis by univariate chi-squared tests against three groups of typical amount and three groups of days of use in the last month. The first page labels the study 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)', level of evidence 1b, but nobody was followed up: the Methods call it a cross-sectional survey (p. 2).
can_establish: What share of a large, self-selected, mostly British online sample of people in the dance-music scene who had used ketamine in the past year reported urinary symptoms they attributed to ketamine in late 2009 (26.6% at least one), which symptoms, whether these reports differed across groups of self-reported typical amount and frequency of use, what respondents recalled about the course of their symptoms after stopping, and how many had sought medical help.
cannot_establish: How common urinary symptoms are among people who use ketamine in general (no sampling frame, no response rate); whether ketamine caused them (no comparison group, symptoms attributed by the respondents themselves, near-universal alcohol and polydrug use, no adjustment); whether symptoms rise steadily with amount or frequency (three-group chi-squared tests, no rates per group, no test for trend); whether the symptoms were brief episodes after a session or persistent (no duration, frequency or severity asked); natural history in the cohort sense (one survey, recalled course, no follow-up despite the 'prospective cohort' label); or any clinical diagnosis (no examination, urine test or validated symptom score).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement (self-selected online survey): through a collaboration with Mixmag, a dance-music publication, the questionnaire was heavily promoted on the website dontstayin.com (the abstract: by a national dance music magazine and website), as part of the group's larger annual survey of drug use and harms among people associated with the dance-music scene (Introduction and Methods, p. 2). Of the 1285 analysed, 80.3% (1032) were from the UK, 11.8% (151) from the USA and 7.9% (102) elsewhere (Results, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All completed surveys; the ketamine and urinary questions were asked only of respondents who reported ketamine use in the last 12 months (Results, p. 2). No other criteria and no checks for repeat responses are reported.
sample.demographics: Of the 1285: mean age 23.5 years (SD 5.8); mean age at first ketamine use 20.42 years (SD 4.3); 70.3% (869) male; 92.6% (1144) white; 73.2% (873) working; 86.7% (1065) heterosexual, 8.5% (105) bisexual, 4.6% (59) homosexual (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). The percentages imply denominators of about 1190 to 1240 rather than 1285 (for example, 869 men at 70.3% implies about 1236; editors' calculation), so some answers were missing; item non-response is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey); item non-response not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Readers of a dance-music magazine's website who chose to respond: no sampling frame, no response rate and no weighting; the authors call the population self-nominating and relatively poorly characterized (Discussion, p. 4). People with urinary problems may have been more or less likely to respond. Last-year use of other drugs and alcohol was almost universal (p. 3). Proportions describe this sample only.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the online questionnaire: lifetime, last-year and last-month use; typical amount per session chosen from fixed amounts; maximum amount in a session; maximum consecutive days of use; days of use in the last month (last-month respondents only); route only for the 307 for whom ketamine was the most recent drug they had tried for the first time (pp. 2–3). No biological verification; the content and purity of what was taken are unknown (p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, grouped by the authors after seeing the distribution of answers. Typical amount per session: 0.125 g or less, 31% (373), called low; 0.25 or 0.5 g, 35%, medium; 1 g or more, 34% (404), high; 4.9% (63) did not know; 5.2% (67) reported regularly taking 3 g or more in a session. Maximum ever in one session: 1 g or more 54.2% (674); 3 g or more 24.6% (307); 5 g or more 6.6% (74). Maximum consecutive days of use: mean 3.5 (mode 2); 11.6% (143) on 7 or more consecutive days. Last-month respondents (792): mean 4.2 days of use in the month (SD 4.87, mode 1), grouped as 1–4 days (70%), 5–8 days (15.6%) and 9 or more days (13.4%). Route (n = 307): 95% intranasal (pp. 2–3). Years of use were not asked; mean age minus mean age at first use is about 3 years (editors' calculation), which is time since first use, not duration of regular use.
exposure.polysubstance: Almost universal and not adjusted for. Last-year use: MDMA 95.5%, cannabis 91.7%, cocaine 78.7%, tobacco 77.5%, mephedrone 66.5%, amphetamine 32%, 'isopropyl nitrate' (poppers, as printed) 27.5%, alcohol 98%. AUDIT-C above the safe-drinking threshold in 87.7% (323) of women and 93.4% (812) of men, and at 8 or more in 35.3% (118) of women and 53.25% (463) of men. Drinking alcohol when taking ketamine: always 31.2% (313), 75% of the time 13.4% (135), 50% 16.3% (165), 25% 20.4% (205), never 18.6% (187) (p. 3). The authors list confounding by other substances and alcohol among the limitations (p. 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. In the question on the course of symptoms, stopping ketamine is self-reported; how long people had stopped for was not asked or is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Urinary symptoms were asked only of respondents who had used ketamine in the last 12 months, and only as symptoms associated with ketamine, so there is no rate among the 2521 respondents who had not used ketamine in the last year (editors' calculation from 3806 and 1285) or among people using the same other drugs. The only contrasts are within the ketamine sample: by typical amount per session, by days of use in the last month and by sex.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Urinary symptoms before ketamine use, urinary tract and sexually transmitted infections, and other conditions that cause the same symptoms were not asked about; the authors say pre-existing pathologies and misattribution cannot be excluded (p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no control group); within the sample, other drug and alcohol use was not compared between people with and without symptoms.

outcomes.instruments: Urinary symptoms: five yes/no items, each a problem the respondent had ever experienced in association with ketamine in the last 12 months: pain in the lower abdomen; burning or stinging when passing urine; needing to pass urine frequently; leakage of urine (incontinence); blood in the urine (Results, 7th paragraph, and Table 1, p. 3). Course of symptoms in relation to ketamine use (improved on stopping; stayed the same while continuing; worse after stopping) and help-seeking (general practitioner; referral to specialist services; accident and emergency) (p. 3). Dependence proxy: the seven DSM-IV dependence criteria, operationalized for the survey, with 3 or more together at some time in the last 12 months counted as dependence, plus markers of problem use (own concern, concern of family or friends, persistent desire or strong urge to use, wish to use less, wish for help to cut down) (p. 3). AUDIT-C, a three-item alcohol screen scored 0–12 (thresholds 3 for women and 4 for men; 8 or more taken to call for assessment for alcohol dependence) (p. 3). All measures are recalled at one time; none was taken during or just after a session.
outcomes.validity_norms: The urinary items and the dependence proxy are not validated, and their exact wording is not printed (the questionnaire is said to be viewable online, p. 2; not read). No validated urinary or bladder-pain symptom score was used, and the duration, frequency and severity of symptoms were not asked, so a single episode after a session counts the same as persistent symptoms. AUDIT-C is a published screen (reference 20).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Urinary symptoms' means a yes to at least one of the five self-attributed items for the last 12 months; 'dependence' means 3 or more of the seven operationalized DSM-IV criteria; 'natural history' means respondents' account, at the one survey, of how their symptoms changed with their use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 15 univariate tests are reported or mentioned (5 symptoms by typical amount, 5 by days of use, the dependence proxy by amount and by days of use, sex by two drinking patterns, sex by symptoms), plus unspecified comparisons of the course of symptoms between high-use and low-use groups (p. 3); no correction and no multivariable model.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without intervals, and chi-squared statistics without degrees of freedom or rates per group. Table 1 (n = 1285): needing to pass urine frequently 17.4% (224); pain in the lower abdomen 11.3% (145); burning or stinging 8.1% (104); leakage 3.3% (43); blood in the urine 1.5% (19); at least one symptom 26.6% (340) (p. 3). Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% interval, n = 1285): at least one symptom about 24.1% to 28.9%; blood in the urine about 0.9% to 2.3%. Typical amount (three groups): burning chi-squared 37.95, frequency 78.29, lower abdominal pain 39.0 (all P < 0.001), blood 6.52 (P = 0.038), leakage 7.44 (P = 0.024). Days of use in the last month (three groups, last-month respondents): lower abdominal pain 52.0 and frequency 39.56 (both P < 0.001), burning 9.8 (P = 0.007); blood 0.62 (P = 0.74) and leakage 5.66 (P = 0.06) not significant (p. 3). The printed P values match 2 degrees of freedom (editors' check), so each test compares three groups without testing a trend. Course of symptoms (n = 251): improved on stopping 51% (128), unchanged while continuing 43% (108), worse after stopping 3.8% (8); help-seeking among the 340 with symptoms: general practitioner 10% (35), specialist referral 2.9% (10), accident and emergency 1.8% (6) (p. 3). Dependence proxy 17% (218), associated with typical amount (chi-squared 170.9) and with days of use (122.3), both P < 0.001 (p. 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported. Ethical approval from the Joint South London and Maudsley and Institute of Psychiatry NHS Research Ethics Committee (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: The symptom rates in each amount and frequency group, on which the dose-response conclusion rests, are not shown; the percentages for the dependence proxy by amount and by frequency are left blank in print; no symptom rate by dependence status is reported, although the Discussion says symptoms are particularly common among respondents with dependence; the Methods name t-tests and Mann-Whitney tests whose results do not appear; the sex comparison of symptoms is reported only as not significant (pp. 2–3).
analysis.power: Not reported. The overall sample is large; the course and help-seeking figures rest on 251 and 340 respondents, and the rarest symptom (blood in the urine) on 19.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1285 self-selected respondents who had used ketamine in the last year, 26.6% (340) said they had had at least one of five urinary symptoms they associated with ketamine in that year, most often needing to pass urine frequently (17.4%) or lower abdominal pain (11.3%); 1.5% (19) reported blood in the urine. Reports differed across three groups of self-reported typical amount for all five symptoms, and across three groups of days of use for three of the five, in univariate tests with no group rates shown. Of 251 who described the course of their symptoms, 128 said they improved when they stopped and 8 that they got worse after stopping; of the 340 with symptoms, 35 had consulted a general practitioner, 10 had been referred to specialist services and 6 had attended an emergency department.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The first page labels the design a prospective cohort with level of evidence 1b; the abstract says a dose and frequency response relationship 'has been shown' and that symptoms are reported in over a quarter of people who use ketamine regularly (p. 1); the summary box says the symptoms may place a considerable demand on primary, secondary and emergency care and may improve once use is decreased (p. 1). The Discussion says the study 'clearly highlights' that urinary harms are dose related and particularly common among respondents with dependence, and that it 'shows the link between ketamine and urinary symptoms' (pp. 3–4). The data are one cross-sectional survey without follow-up; 26.6% is among anyone who used in the past year (70% of last-month respondents used on 1–4 days), not among people who use regularly; no group rates or trend tests are shown, so a graded dose-response is not demonstrated; no symptom rates by dependence status are reported; the recalled course concerns stopping, not reducing; and 'considerable demand' rests on 35, 10 and 6 people. With no comparison group and symptoms attributed by the respondents, the survey shows that respondents linked these symptoms to ketamine, not that ketamine caused them. The Limitations acknowledge self-selection, unknown content, polydrug and alcohol use and possible misattribution (p. 4).

timeline.event: Shahani et al.: first case series naming ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis (9 patients, Toronto).

Muetzelfeldt et al.: 90 people who used ketamine (frequent, infrequent and former); cystitis-like symptoms in 20% of the frequent and 6.7% of the infrequent group, and urinary symptoms in 13.3% of the former group (as cited, p. 4 of the online-first PDF; not read).
Cottrell and Gillatt: survey of UK urologists; about one-third of cases resolved after stopping, one-third stayed the same and one-third may progress (as cited, p. 4; not read).
Ng et al.: 233 emergency-department presentations after ketamine use in Hong Kong, 12% with urinary symptoms (as cited, p. 4; not read).
This survey: 26.6% of 1285 respondents who had used ketamine in the last year reported at least one urinary symptom they associated with ketamine.
Chan et al., Hong Kong Medical Journal: systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine-associated uropathy (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The authors place their figure beside a smaller UK study whose frequent group reported cystitis-like symptoms at a similar rate (20%) and beside a urologists' survey of outcomes after stopping (p. 4); both are cited, not read. Later surveys and the systematic review of Chan et al. (2022) are to be appraised. Prevalence figures from self-selected online samples are not comparable with population estimates.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement or acknowledgments (pp. 1–5 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: 'None declared' (Conflict of interest, p. 4 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Addiction CAG, South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and St George's Hospital Medical School, London; Bristol Urological Institute, Southmead Hospital, Bristol (p. 1). The survey is the group's annual dance-music drug survey run with Mixmag, with the questionnaires hosted at globaldrugsurvey.com/mixmag (p. 2). The two urologist authors had earlier published on ketamine-associated urinary tract pathology (references 11 and 22, p. 5). In a later Global Drug Survey paper the first author declared that he founded and directs Global Drug Survey (Winstock et al., 2013, p. 6; card sc_winstock_2013); no such statement appears here. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who use ketamine, recruited from a known sampling frame, with validated urinary symptom scores, the duration and severity of symptoms, testing to confirm use, and a comparison group who use the same other drugs and alcohol but not ketamine, reassessed over time and after people stop, with symptom rates reported by amount and frequency and adjusted for alcohol and other drugs.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No sampling frame: readers of a dance-music magazine's website who chose to respond.
Self-nominating convenience sample, described in the abstract as purposeful sampling (p. 1).
1285 respondents; the any-symptom proportion has a 95% interval of about 24% to 29% (editors' calculation). The course-of-symptoms and help-seeking figures rest on 251 and 340.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Countries, demographics and other drug use are given, but denominators vary without explanation, the survey dates conflict between abstract and Results, and the question wording is not printed.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Item non-response is not reported; who the 251 describing their course were is not stated; the frequency comparisons can include only the 792 last-month respondents.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Five unvalidated self-report items in which respondents attributed symptoms to ketamine, without duration, severity, examination or urine testing; dependence by an unvalidated proxy.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same online questions for all, but recall over 12 months and self-attribution may differ between people, and route was asked of only 307.

No intervals; three-group chi-squared tests without group rates or trend tests; no adjustment for alcohol or other drugs; no correction for multiple tests; several sets of figures do not add up (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Open online survey with no denominator; covered under items 1 and 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of what a large self-selected sample of people in the dance-music scene who had used ketamine reported in late 2009, the survey is informative and was one of the first to count ketamine-attributed urinary symptoms outside clinics. Its figures cannot be generalized (no frame, no response rate), the symptoms are self-attributed, unvalidated and of unknown duration, and the dose and frequency associations are univariate three-group tests with no rates shown and no allowance for near-universal alcohol and polydrug use. It may be cited for the proportions in this sample (26.6% with at least one symptom, and the five items), for the self-reported course in 251 respondents and for help-seeking among 340, each labelled as self-report in a self-selected online sample. It may not be cited for a population prevalence, for ketamine as the cause, for a demonstrated graded dose-response, for symptom rates among people meeting the dependence proxy, or for natural history followed over time.

key_findings.finding: Survey and sample: 3806 surveys were completed; 1947 (51.1%) respondents had ever used ketamine and 1285 (33.8%) had used it in the last 12 months; only the 1285 were asked the ketamine and urinary questions. The abstract dates the survey November 2009 to January 2010; the Results give 17 November 2010 to 4 January 2010.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Patients and methods and Results (p. 1); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2, right column)
key_findings.note: The Results' start date falls after its end date; the abstract's November 2009 start is probably right, but the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: The 1285: 80.3% (1032) from the UK, 11.8% (151) from the USA, 7.9% (102) elsewhere; mean age 23.5 years (SD 5.8); mean age at first ketamine use 20.42 years (SD 4.3); 70.3% (869) male; 92.6% (1144) white; 73.2% (873) working.

Self-reported typical amount per session, grouped by the authors: 0.125 g or less 31% (373); 0.25 or 0.5 g 35%; 1 g or more 34% (404); 4.9% (63) could not say; 5.2% (67) regularly took 3 g or more in a session. Maximum ever in one session: 1 g or more 54.2% (674), 3 g or more 24.6% (307), 5 g or more 6.6% (74).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, right column, continuing on p. 3, left column)
key_findings.note: Respondents' reports, measured by the study; not doses given. 74 is 6.6% only of about 1120; against the roughly 1245 implied by the other two maximum-amount figures it is about 5.9% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Frequency: maximum consecutive days of use mean 3.5 (mode 2), with 11.6% (143) having used on 7 or more consecutive days; the 792 who had used in the last month did so on a mean of 4.2 days (SD 4.87, mode 1), grouped as 1–4 days (70%), 5–8 days (15.6%) and 9 or more days (13.4%). Route was asked only of the 307 for whom ketamine was the most recent drug they had tried for the first time: 95% intranasal.

Dependence proxy: 17% (218) reported 3 or more of the seven operationalized DSM-IV dependence criteria together in the last 12 months; of the 792 who had used in the last month, 22.7% (180) wanted to use less and 5.9% (47) wanted help; the proxy was associated with typical amount (chi-squared 170.9, P < 0.001) and with days of use per month (chi-squared 122.3, P < 0.001), with the percentages left blank in print.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (left column, continuing in the middle column)
key_findings.note: The authors say the self-report proxy may overestimate dependence (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 4).

key_findings.finding: Other drugs and alcohol in the last year: MDMA 95.5%, cannabis 91.7%, cocaine 78.7%, tobacco 77.5%, mephedrone 66.5%, amphetamine 32%, 'isopropyl nitrate' (poppers, as printed) 27.5%, alcohol 98%. AUDIT-C above the safe-drinking threshold: women 87.7% (323), men 93.4% (812); 8 or more: women 35.3% (118), men 53.25% (463). Alcohol with ketamine: always 31.2% (313), 75% of the time 13.4% (135), 50% 16.3% (165), 25% 20.4% (205), never 18.6% (187).
key_findings.note: The sex-specific figures for drinking with ketamine (44.6% of men against 31.6% of women always or 75% of the time; 30.8% of women against 21.0% of men never) cannot be reconciled with these totals (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 1, urinary symptoms respondents associated with ketamine in the last 12 months (n = 1285): needing to pass urine frequently 17.4% (224); pain in the lower abdomen 11.3% (145); burning or stinging when passing urine 8.1% (104); leakage of urine (incontinence) 3.3% (43); blood in the urine 1.5% (19). At least one symptom: 340 (26.6%). No significant difference between men and women in any symptom (chi-squared; no figures given).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 7th paragraph (middle column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: 340 of 1285 is 26.5% (editors' calculation). The items ask whether a problem was ever experienced in the year, not its duration or severity.

key_findings.finding: By self-reported typical amount (three groups), higher amounts went with higher rates of burning or stinging (chi-squared 37.95, P < 0.001), needing to pass urine frequently (78.29, P < 0.001), lower abdominal pain (39.0, P < 0.001), blood in the urine (6.52, P = 0.038) and leakage of urine (7.44, P = 0.024).
key_findings.note: Symptom rates per amount group are not given; the P values match 2 degrees of freedom (editors' check), a three-group comparison rather than a test for trend.

key_findings.finding: By days of use in the last month (three groups), more frequent use went with higher rates of lower abdominal pain (chi-squared 52.0, P < 0.001), needing to pass urine frequently (39.56, P < 0.001) and burning or stinging (9.8, P = 0.007), but not with blood in the urine (0.62, P = 0.74) or leakage of urine (5.66, P = 0.06).
key_findings.note: Rates per group are not given. The frequency groups are defined among the 792 who had used in the last month (Results, 4th paragraph), so these tests can include at most 792 of the 1285.

key_findings.finding: Of 251 respondents who described their symptoms over time in relation to their ketamine use, 51% (128) reported improvement when they stopped, 43% (108) that symptoms had stayed the same while they continued to use, and 3.8% (8) that symptoms got worse after stopping; none of these outcomes differed significantly between the high-use and low-use groups.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (p. 3, right column); Abstract, Results (p. 1)
key_findings.note: 8 of 251 is 3.2%, and 128 + 108 + 8 = 244, leaving 7 unaccounted for (editors' calculation); how many of the 251 had stopped is not given.

key_findings.finding: Of the 340 respondents with urinary symptoms, 10% (35) had sought help from their general practitioner, 2.9% (10) had been referred to specialist services and 1.8% (6) had attended an accident and emergency department.

Other studies as cited in the Discussion: in a cohort of 90 people who used ketamine, cystitis-like symptoms were reported by 20% of the frequent and 6.7% of the infrequent group, and urinary symptoms by 13.3% of the former group; a survey of UK urologists found that about one-third of cases resolved after stopping, one-third stayed the same and one-third may progress; in one study 12% of people presenting to emergency departments after recent ketamine use had urinary symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (left column, the 4th continuing in the middle column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a self-nominating, relatively poorly characterized population; self-reported experiences with a substance of uncertain composition; high polydrug use and confounding by other substances; uncertain dose quantification and purity; route unknown for most, so a higher risk with injecting cannot be excluded; symptom misattribution, other substance use, acute polydrug or alcohol use, or pre-existing pathologies cannot be excluded; the dependence figure may be an overestimate because of self-report and a proxy measure.

Authors' conclusions: the study clearly highlights that urinary harms are dose related and particularly common among respondents with dependence; symptoms go with more frequent use and larger amounts per session; in most, stopping goes with cessation or improvement of symptoms, which may persist while use continues and in a few progress after stopping; the study shows the link between ketamine and urinary symptoms; people who use ketamine and primary-care providers need education, and a multidisciplinary approach promoting harm reduction, cessation and early referral is needed. The first page labels the study 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)', level of evidence 1b.
key_findings.locator: Study type box and Conclusions (p. 1); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 3, right column, continuing on p. 4) and 8th paragraph (p. 4, right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the survey period as November 2009 to January 2010; the Results say the surveys were completed between 17 November 2010 and 4 January 2010, a start date after the end date.
reporting_issues.consequence: The field period is uncertain; most likely 17 November 2009 to 4 January 2010, but the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: The first page labels the study type 'Symptom prevalence (prospective cohort)' with level of evidence 1b; the Methods describe an online cross-sectional survey, and no respondent was followed up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The natural-history figures were recalled at one survey; claims must not describe them as prospective or cohort findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The 8 respondents whose symptoms worsened after stopping are given as 3.8% of 251 in the abstract and the Results; by the editors' calculation, 8 of 251 is 3.2%, and the three outcome groups (128 + 108 + 8 = 244) leave 7 of the 251 unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the 3.8% is unclear (8 is 3.8% of about 210); cite the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The 340 respondents with at least one symptom are given as 26.6% of 1285; by the editors' calculation, 340 of 1285 is 26.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; perhaps a denominator of about 1278 after missing answers.

reporting_issues.issue: Overall, 44.6% always or 75% of the time drank alcohol with ketamine (31.2% + 13.4%) and 18.6% never did; the sex-specific figures are 44.6% of men against 31.6% of women for always or 75% of the time, and 21.0% of men against 30.8% of women for never. An overall share cannot equal the men's figure when the women's is lower, nor lie below both sexes' figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one set of drinking-with-ketamine figures is wrong; neither the totals nor the sex comparison should be cited without this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: For women, 323 above the AUDIT-C threshold is given as 87.7% and 118 scoring 8 or more as 35.3%; by the editors' calculation, these imply about 368 and about 334 women respectively.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the two figures use different, unstated denominators.

reporting_issues.issue: Among maximum amounts ever used in a session, 674 is given as 54.2%, 307 as 24.6% and 74 as 6.6%; by the editors' calculation, the first two imply a denominator of about 1245 and the third about 1120, and 74 of about 1245 would be 5.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one of the figures is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The association of the dependence proxy with typical amount and with frequency is printed with the percentages missing, as '(%, χ2 = 170.9 ...)' and '(%, χ2 = 122.3 ...)'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the association cannot be read; only the test statistics are available.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name unpaired t-tests and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables; no result of either is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Analyses may have been done and not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says urinary harms are particularly common among respondents with dependence, but the Results give no urinary symptom figures by dependence status.
reporting_issues.consequence: That statement has no data behind it in the paper and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion speaks of over a quarter of people who use ketamine regularly, but the 26.6% is among everyone who used ketamine in the last 12 months, including the 70% of last-month respondents who used on 1–4 days and, by the editors' calculation (1285 minus 792), 493 who had not used it in the last month.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is a past-year figure for any use, not a figure for regular use.

Read in full, including Table 1, the conflict-of-interest statement and the references; born-digital PDF; all numbers checked on 150-dpi renderings of pp. 1–5.
